1:
The command is to go again, and the shape of the chapter is settled first. Keil and Delitzsch divide it into the symbolical action and its explanation, with the announcement of the reformation the action is meant to effect, and hold the purely symbolical character of the command evident from the command itself. Calvin is blunter: those are too gross in their notions who think the prophet married a harlot. It was a vision, a picture set before the people's eyes in which they might see their own conduct. Henry hears in the repetition a rule of method: for the conviction of sinners precept must be upon precept and line upon line, and if one sign will not persuade, another must be tried.

Who the woman is, and which people she stands for, is not settled. Ellicott takes her for the daughter of Diblaim, the prophet's own wife, now another man's concubine slave and perhaps destitute. Clarke keeps the two commands apart: the earlier one showed the infidelity of the kingdom and God's divorce of it, while this woman is a lawful wife who joined a paramour, was divorced, and now repents without being reconciled — the exact state of the people under the Babylonian captivity, separated from their idols yet still separated from their God. Henry reports the view that the chapter belongs to the two tribes, since this woman is not divorced but left desolate and afterwards returns, and rejects it because those addressed are called the children of Israel.

The phrase rendered beloved of her friend carries a dispute the commentators settle by pointing. Clarke explains that the same consonants give either a friend or evil according to how they are pointed, so that the clause may be read loving another or a lover of evil, and prefers the first. Ellicott agrees, renders it loved by another, and sets aside the Greek reading a lover of evil as resting on a different text. Calvin takes the word for husband outright, citing another prophet's figure of a woman departing from her partner, and draws an aggravation from it: a wife kindly used has less excuse than one who can plead her husband's severity. Wesley says simply, her husband.

Calvin makes most of the verb. The prophet is not told to take a wife but to love a woman, and the difference is the whole comfort of the chapter: before restoring the people from exile God loved them in their widowhood. The prediction stands between the earlier denunciation and the promise of pardon, correcting the mistake that being received again means the chastisement is cancelled. Henry works the same ground from the other side, astonished that so much love should be thrown away on so unworthy a people, and concluding that in goodwill to sinners God's thoughts are not ours and his compassion more condescending than any man's breast would admit.

The flagons raise a question of substance and a question of meaning. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott read the word as cakes: raisin-cakes, or the luscious grape-cakes used in idol worship, which Ellicott takes as generally descriptive of the licentious accompaniments of the Ashtoreth rites. Clarke allows either, flagons used for libations and drunk at idol feasts, or cakes of dried grapes, sweet cakes, consecrated wafers. Wesley keeps the drink and the feast. Henry makes it a moral observation, that idolatry and sensuality go together and those who make a god of the belly will make one of anything, noting that the priests drank no wine when they went in to minister. Calvin reads the whole as drunkenness, and says grapes rather than wine because gorged drinkers grow nauseated and must find new arts to recover the taste, which is exactly how the superstitious behave, forever after novelty and never at rest.
2:
The price is worked out in several currencies and does not come to one sum. Gill makes fifteen shekels about one pound seventeen and sixpence at half a crown the shekel, half a servant's price, and takes the verb for bargaining after a rabbi, though he notes the Latin version renders it I dug her, and thinks hired the better word, the Arabic for hire being the same. Clarke reckons about two pounds five, and the grain at twelve or thirteen bushels; Wesley says fourteen. Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott add the grain to the silver: fifteen ephahs at a shekel each makes thirty shekels in all, the compensation the law set for a slave gored by an ox, which Ellicott takes as a hint of how far the woman had sunk.

Calvin will not let the smallness be read as generosity. Respectable women did not live on barley; the prophet gave coarse food and little of it, and those who elicit from it that God would keep the adulteress sumptuously go against the whole design. He turns it into a rule for husbands: one who pardons at once with a smiling countenance and lays aside his authority ruins his wife by levity, while one who forgives but holds her strictly to duty shows no common prudence. Jerome's arithmetic, fifteen because they left Egypt on the fifteenth day and forty-five bushels because the law came forty-five days after, he dismisses as puerile trifles.

What the prophet then promises her divides them. Keil and Delitzsch describe detention rather than marriage, sitting meaning to remain quiet, the phrase for me showing the restraint imposed out of affection, to train her up as a faithful wife; opinions differ, they add, whether the prophet is himself included in the prohibition, and they think not. Ellicott holds he is: the closing clause is better rendered I will also be to thee, meaning he too will have no intercourse with her, and cites two rabbis for it. Calvin reads the words the opposite way, as a pledge: he subscribes himself her husband and binds himself in turn, so the widowhood is a mutual compact, not an abandonment. Clarke keeps it practical: no home, a contract, and money and barley to keep temptation off.

The deprivations are counted as pairs: Keil and Delitzsch take king and prince for civil government, offering and monument for worship, and ephod with teraphim, noting that the monuments were consecrated to Baal and forbidden by name in the law. Ellicott finds the two cults deliberately intermingled and reads image as upright stones standing for Baal. Clarke observes that the old versions read altar for image, taking one word for another that differs by a letter, that a manuscript has oblation, and that some would read seraphim for teraphim; in exile, he concludes, they were as wholly without idolatrous forms as without God's worship. Calvin asks why an ephod is named when the priesthood continued in the south, and answers that the northern king built his worship to resemble the true as closely as he could.

How long the many days run is the sharpest split. Calvin holds the number is simply the seventy years another prophet afterwards fixed, and that this one does not go beyond it. Gill counts seven hundred years from the Assyrian captivity to Christ, and nineteen hundred more since. Clarke calls it literally fulfilled since the Romans destroyed the temple, with neither king nor prince nor priest nor oracle for nearly eighteen hundred years, and expects it to run until they acknowledge as their Saviour the one they crucified. Wesley keeps to the exile, where strangers rule, the images cannot be carried and the conquerors allow no new ones. Henry ends where the parable does: the widow is at length received, and we fear not the majesty only but the goodness.
5:
The return is first a return of the heart. Gill takes the children of Israel to cover the ten tribes and the two together, following a rabbi who reads the name so, and insists it means more than a return to their own land: they repent of their course of life, and particularly of rejecting the true Messiah, discard their traditions, renounce their own righteousness and believe for life and salvation. Calvin finds here the fruit of the chastisement, and the answer to any complaint that God was too severe: had he stretched out his hand at once there would have been no repentance in them, whereas cleansed by long correction they confess him sincerely. He notes too that the prophet does not say they shall seek God but Jehovah their God, setting the one true name against the Baals and carrying an implied reproof, that they had gone after superstitions though God had brought them up as a father his children in his bosom.

Seeking the Lord and seeking David are one act. Keil and Delitzsch argue it from history: the falling away from the house of David was the effect of an inward apostasy, openly declared in the setting up of the calves, so a true return cannot happen without a return to David, to whose seed the kingdom was promised for ever. Ellicott reads David as the predicted representative of the dynasty, the name being used of a later house in the same way, and finds the fulfilment only in the Messianic reign. Calvin agrees that the man was long dead and that the prophet sets forth an everlasting kingdom in one person, the promise being that the throne should last as long as sun and moon shine. Wesley says plainly, the Messiah who is the son of David.

Clarke argues the identification by elimination. He cites the Targum, that they shall obey the Messiah the son of David, and disposes of the alternatives: the family of David will not do, since the northern house was scarcely ever submissive to him and never acknowledged his line after Solomon; Zerubbabel will not do, since the short and imperfect obedience given him cannot answer the high terms of the prophecy. From the prophecies, from the facts, from the rabbis themselves and from the later scriptures he concludes that the texts apply solely to Jesus, and remarks on the propensity of some to deny such evidences while professing the doctrines.

Calvin declines an argument that would have served him. Some, he says with more refinement, contend that Christ must be Jehovah because the prophet makes him sought as God is sought; Calvin judges this insufficient to settle the dispute and takes the passage more simply, that seeking means fleeing under the guardianship of a legitimate king divinely ordained, so that they seek their God in the person of the king. On the fear he is equally careful. The verb can mean to dread and lose all courage, but here it must be taken well, for God means not to be dreaded but to allure them sweetly, so that they obey freely and even joyfully. Majesty by itself only sends us to look for hiding places; it is a taste of goodness that makes reverence possible, and the goodness itself he refers to Christ, rejecting the reading that takes the word for glory.

When the latter days fall is left open. Ellicott takes the phrase indefinitely, of the distant future, the horizon of the seer's gaze. Wesley makes them gospel times. Clarke puts the end of the long darkness there and not before. Calvin dates their beginning earlier, at the moment liberty was granted to return home, while insisting that a continued series must be understood from the return down to the coming of Christ, when the Lord performed more fully what is here declared.
